verses.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame in connection with the LORD's name, she came to test him with hard questions.
She arrived in Jerusalem with a huge caravan of camels carrying spices, a great deal of gold, and precious stones. When she met Solomon, she talked with him about everything on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. There was nothing she asked that the king couldn't explain.
The queen of Sheba saw Solomon's wisdom and the palace he had built.
She saw the food on his table, the seating of his servants, how his officials attended him, their clothes, his cupbearers, and the way he went up to the LORD's house. It took her breath away.
She told the king, “The report I heard at home about your deeds and your wisdom was true.
I didn't believe it until I came and saw it myself. I'd been told less than half of it! Your wisdom and prosperity go beyond what I heard.
How fortunate your people are! How fortunate your servants are to stand before you every day and hear your wisdom!
Praise the LORD your God, who delighted in you and put you on Israel's throne. Because the LORD loves Israel forever, he made you king to do what is just and right.”
She gave King Solomon a hundred and twenty talents of gold, a huge amount of spices, and precious stones. No one ever brought him as many spices again as the queen of Sheba did.
Hiram's fleet, which brought gold from Ophir, also brought large quantities of almug wood and precious stones from there.

The king used the almug wood to make pillars for the LORD's house and the palace, and harps and other stringed instruments for the singers. Nothing like that almug wood has arrived or been seen since.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she asked for, as well as the generous gifts he chose to give her as king. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
Solomon received six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold in a year,
besides what came from traders, merchants, the kings of the various peoples, and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold, using six hundred shekels of gold for each one.
He also made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold, using three minas of gold for each. The king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a great ivory throne and covered it with the finest gold.
Six steps led up to the throne, which had a rounded top at the back. The seat had an armrest on either side, with a lion standing beside each armrest.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one on each side of every step. No other kingdom had made anything like it.
All King Solomon's drinking cups were gold, and all the vessels in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. None were silver, because silver was considered worth little in Solomon's time.
The king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with Hiram's fleet. Once every three years his fleet came back with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon surpassed every other king on earth in wealth and wisdom.
People from all over the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart.
Year after year each visitor brought a gift: silver and gold vessels, clothes, armor, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen until he had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot towns and kept some with him in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem and cedar as common as sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Solomon's horses came from Egypt. The king's merchants bought them in herds at an agreed price.
A chariot imported from Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse cost a hundred and fifty. The merchants also exported them to the Hittite and Syrian kings.
